newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Brooklyn Dodgers fantasy will not fade.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Brooklyn Dodgers fantasy will not fade.

text.p: The fantasy refuses to die in the minds of people in Brooklyn and beyond: the Dodgers come home.

To listen to any Brooklynite -- former players and their fans -- or visit Brooklyn's History Museum or The Brooklyn Dodger sports bar is to understand the love for a special baseball team affectionately known as "Dem Bums."

The pain of the departure 40 years ago to Los Angeles is always traumatically described as having "ripped the heart and soul out of Brooklyn" or as the worst day in history, aside from the outbreak of the Second World War.

Many Brooklynites trembled with excitement and dreamed of seeing their team play in Brooklyn again after Los Angeles Dodgers owner Peter O'Malley announced on Jan. 6 that he was selling the club. On the subway, in bars, in newspaper columns and on radio and television, they have let out a cry from the heart: "We gotta bring Dem Bums back to Brooklyn!"
"It's a fantasy at best, but what a great fantasy," said Marty Adler, president of the Brooklyn Dodgers Hall of Fame organisation. "The Dodgers were the pulse of the borough."

In their 1940s and 50s heyday, the Dodgers played in seven World Series against the dominant dynasty of the New York Yankees -- those pin-striped players from a faroff New York borough called the Bronx -- and won only once, in 1955.

"There was an underdog mentality, we were smaller than the big city Yankees," said former pitcher Ralph Branca, now 70, who is best known for giving up a home run to Bobby Thomson that won the 1951 National League pennant for the New York Giants. Dubbed by locals "the shot heard around the world," the moment still gives Dodgers fans nightmares.
A LOVE AFFAIR
"The people of Brooklyn were all rooting for the Dodgers, it was more than just fans getting behind a team," Branca said. "It was a love affair."

He and others recall a community of ethnic groups from all over the world pouring out of homes and factories in the middle of the day to support the team at Ebbets Field. The stadium was torn down and replaced by housing projects when the club went west in 1957, and the decline of the borough as a centre for industry and jobs is often linked with the departure of the Dodgers.
But Brooklyn dreams on.
Roger Kahn, author of "The Boys of Summer" about the 1955 champion Dodgers, wrote a fantasy column in the New York Daily News last week on how the Dodgers came home to Brooklyn.

Datelined "Brooklyn, N.Y., Oct. 26, 2007," Kahn's column is a "history" of the Dodgers' return and a World Series against the Yankees at "Robinson Field," named after Dodgers second baseman Jackie Robinson, who became the first black man to play in the Major Leagues when he signed in 1947.
The Yankees win. "What were you expecting here in Brooklyn, a miracle?" Kahn asked.
Everyone knows it would take a miracle, but they indulge in the fantasy nevertheless.
UNDERDOGS BEAT LOS ANGELES FRANCHISE
Wounded Brooklynites like to remind the world of the grave injustice done to them when the O'Malley family moved their beloved team to Tinsel Town.

"Part of the mystique is that even though you weren't born at the time fathers told their sons, who then told their sons," said David Senatore, co-owner of The Brooklyn Dodger bar in the blue-collar Bay Ridge neighbourhood. "Maybe you weren't there but you heard it around the dinner table many times."

Four years ago, The Brooklyn Dodger bar owners exemplified the underdog mentality that Branca remembers. The Los Angeles Dodgers franchise sued them for trademark infringement, but the bar fought back and a judge ruled what everyone here already knew -- the Dodgers had abandoned the borough in 1957 and therefore their right to the trademark name.

A large picture of Ebbets Field adorns most of one wall of the bar. A Dodger uniform and Jackie Robinson's bat are in glass cases behind the counter, along with a T-shirt proclaiming: "Brooklyn's Back. Brooklyn 1, L.A. 0" to commemorate the 1993 lawsuit victory.

O'Malley's financial windfall from moving to Los Angeles and reaping the rewards of a wealthy franchise became the model for how baseball clubs grew into big businesses. And many Brooklynites have neither forgotten nor forgiven.
NO PRAYER FOR O'MALLEY

At Brooklyn's Historical Museum, where visitors are invited to offer comments on the displays devoted to the Dodgers, one wrote: "My father was taken by his Pa the year Ebbets Field opened. I was 19 when the Dodgers left. I've since become a priest and, God forgive me, I didn't pray for Walter O'Malley when he went to our maker."
No story about Brooklyn or the character of its people can be told without including Dodgers lore.

In the 1995 movie "Blue in the Face" about the lives of a Brooklyn smoke shop manager and his friends, 1970s rock musician Lou Reed says, "It was probably a childhood trauma that I had, other than the Dodgers leaving Brooklyn, which, if you think about it, is a reason why some of us are imbued with a cynicism that we never recovered from."
The filmmakers even had the ghost of Jackie Robinson visit the owner of the Brooklyn Cigar Company when he was grappling with a decision over selling the small smoke shop.
"I was the man who changed America, Vinnie, and I did it all right here in Brooklyn ... although they spat at me, cursed me, made my life a living hell," Robinson's ghost says.
